analytic.title: A Voltage and Resource Synthesis Technique for Energy-Aware Real-time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: We consider a resource synthesis technique for realtime systems where dynamic voltage scaling is supported, the energy budget is limited, and the performance of the system depends on how resources and energy are used. We propose a resource synthesis technique that derives both the supply voltages and the resource allocation of the tasks in the system to maximize system performance. The resulting system satisfies real-time schedulability and energy requirements.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Optimizing energy usage becomes more important for the devices from the mobile devices to the satellites where energy is limited and costly. Optimal energy usage can be interpreted in many ways. Low energy or low power consumption is the primary goal for optimal energy or power usage. However, when the energy is refreshed periodically and any surplus energy that the battery cannot store is simply wasted, low energy consumption is not always desirable. Energy-aware resource usage is another approach that makes use of the energy efficiently. It includes both low energy consumption and proactive consumption of any extra energy for better system performance. For example, in the case of some signal processing systems, any extra energy can be used to increase the quality of the output by increasing input sampling rate and processing rate.

There are various techniques for power optimization. Several power optimization techniques in embedded systems are in [1][10] [11]. Voltage scaling enables efficient energy usage at the expense of the latency and speed changes [3]. Voltage synthesis techniques and scheduling techniques for a low-energy real-time system are in [1][7] [12] [15]. Power aware voltage scaling techniques for real-time systems are in [4] [14][8].

This paper considers an energy-aware resource synthesis problem for real-time systems that have the following characteristics. (1) Dynamic voltage scaling is supported. The supply voltage of a task can be independently set. (2) Each task has dynamic performance. The performance of a task depends on either the effective execution time it runs (variable execution time) or how frequently it is executed (variable frequency). Performance models based on variable execution time include Increasing Reward with Increasing Service (IRIS) model [5] and Imprecise Computation model [6]. The variable frequency model is often used for control systems [16]. These two performance models are shown as integrated into a resource-based performance model under some real-time schedulers [9], which is equivalent to the QoS-based Resource Allocation Model (Q-RAM) [13]. In this paper, each task is associated with a resourcebased performance function that is a function of two independent variables, the supply voltage and the normalized resource utilization at the reference voltage.
(3) Hard real-time systems are considered, and each task must complete its execution by its deadline. ( 4) System-wide energy is limited and wasted if not used.

We present an efficient resource synthesis technique deriving the supply voltage and the normalized resource utilization of a task for maximum system performance under an energy budget. Our approach is an extension of the previous research on resource synthesis techniques [9] that do not consider dynamic voltage scaling technique. This paper also extends the performance model with dynamic voltage scaling.

The contributions of the technique in this paper are as follows. Our technique considers the system where dynamic voltage scaling is supported and each task has a dynamic performance model. Our technique synthesizes the resource share and the supply voltage of a task for maximum system performance. Our technique is distinguished from the other voltage synthesis techniques [4][7] and resource allocation techniques [13] [16] in that our technique models voltage and the effective resource share of a task as two independent variables and synthesizes them at the same time. To our knowledge, our technique is unique to consider those two parameters independently and synthesize both for maximum system performance. As shown in our previous research, optimal resource allocation without considering the voltage scaling technique itself is a non-trivial problem [9]. Considering the voltage of a task makes room for more improvement in energy usage but it also complicates the problem. However, the technique presented in this paper derives the voltages and resource share of a task with little more complexity than our previous resource synthesis technique that did not consider voltages as a design parameter [9].

The remainder of this paper is as follows. The system model and an overview of the problems are discussed in Section 2 followed by a motivational example. We discuss some assumptions and a mathematical modeling of the problem. The analysis technique for a single static voltage for all tasks is given in Section 3. In Section 4, we present the analysis technique deriving independent voltage for the tasks and the solution of the motivational example. Section 5 concludes the paper with a summary and a discussion of future studies.

div.p: A set of independent tasks {τ 1 , τ 2 , .., τ N } exists in a single CPU system. Each task has its own characteristics: the frequency of execution f i , the execution time t i ref at the reference voltage, the energy consumption per execution instance e i ref at the reference voltage, and the performance function (φ i ). Throughout this paper, we call the normalized execution time at the reference voltage the effective execution time of a task. Likewise, we call the normalized resource utilization of a task at the reference voltage as the effective resource utilization of the task. The performance function of a task is a method of determining a reward function for running the task. We consider non-decreasing concave performance functions. System-wide performance is the sum of the performance of each task. The resource utilization ρ i (v i ) allocated to task τ i at voltage v i is the product of its execution time and frequency and it can be driven from the effective resource utilization ref i ρ using (Eq.3). The energy consumption E of the system is limited by total energy available E max within a time interval T.

div.p: Two different performance models for variable execution time and variable frequency considered in [9] assume no voltage scaling. The Variable Frequency (VF) model assumes a fixed execution time with a variable frequency. The Variable Execution Time (VET) model assumes a variable execution time with a fixed frequency. Under the VET model, we assume that energy consumption of a task is linearly proportional to its execution time. It is presented that the two models can be integrated into a single model using a performance function based on the resource utilization under some real-time scheduling policies [9]. Those scheduling polices include Earliest Deadline First (EDF), Least Laxity First (LLF), Rate Monotonic (RM), and Rate Monotonic-Harmonic (RM-H), for which schedulability analysis can be done with total resource utilization.

The models extend to consider dynamic voltage systems as follows. Under the VF model, each task has a range of operating frequency f i,min ≤ f i,min ≤ f i,max but has a fixed execution time t i ref at the reference voltage.

Our goal is to find processor utilization allocations and corresponding supply voltage(s) such that (1) system performance is maximized, (2) the system is schedulable, and (3) the energy consumption is within the energy budget. The resource utilization of a task is a function of execution time and frequency. Either the execution time or the frequency can be a free variable depending on the model used. Throughout this paper, we assume the EDF policy for real-time scheduling and the total resource utilization available ρ max is 1.0.

We also assume the use of an ideal on-off energy saving technique and that energy is not wasted when system is idle. This assumption is realistic when the system load is very high, and the idle time is very small.

We attack the problem in two steps. First, we consider a system having a single voltage in which all tasks run at the same voltage. Deriving the system voltage and the resource allocations for the tasks for maximum system performance is considered in Section 3. Second, a more flexible system is considered where each task runs on its own supply voltage. Deriving the supply voltages and the resource allocations for the tasks are considered in Section 4.

div.head: Single Static Voltage System
div.p: In this section, we consider a system for which a supply voltage within a given range can be chosen at design time, but cannot be changed dynamically. This model works well when the set of the tasks does not change at run-time and where dynamic voltage scaling is too costly to implement.

div.head: Solution
div.p: We proposed a fast resource synthesis technique for systems with predetermined supply voltage [9]. In this section we present an extended resource synthesis technique that derives the supply voltage of the system in addition to resource utilizations.

To simplify our illustration, we reduce the three dimensional search space into a two dimensional plane by shrinking the voltage axis that is shown in Figure 2a. Now, a point in Figure 2a may correspond to multiple voltages. By Lemma 1, an optimal solution resides on the bold lines where (ρ = ρ max and 0 < E ≤ E max ) or (0 < ρ ≤ ρ max and E = E max ) unless an optimal solution lies inside of area D in Figure 2a. Let the point s in Figure 2a be the point where v = V min and ρ i = ρ i,min (V min ) for each task τ i . At the point s, both the system performance and the energy usage are minimal.

div.head: General case:
div.p: The search starts at the point s where both the performance and the energy consumption are minimum where v = V min and ρ i = ρ i,min (V min ) for each task τ i . In the nontrivial case, the start point s may reside in area A or area D. Let the bold lines belong to area D for the purpose of illustration. We start with the case where the start point lies in area A.

When the start point s lies in area A, the system is over-utilized but energy is under-used. Energy is traded with resource utilization by increasing the supply voltage until the resource utilization becomes equal to ρ max , which is shown as the arrow to the point s 1 labeled as a 1 in Figure 2a. If the resulting is V ref and the resource utilization is ρ max , the search is finished. It is an optimal solution. If the resulting energy consumption is larger than E max , no solution exists. Otherwise, we increase the voltage further until either the supply voltage becomes V ref or the available energy is reduced by half (E max -E 2 = E 2 -E 1 ), which is heuristically chosen. The process is shown as the arrow labeled as a 2 to the point s 2 in Figure 2a. So far there are no performance changes, because there are no changes in the effective resource allocations of the tasks. From s 2 , we increase the resource allocation of the tasks, which increases performance, resource utilization, and energy consumption, until either the resource utilization becomes its maximum value, ρ max , as shown by the arrow a 3.1 or the energy consumption reaches its maximum E max as shown by the arrow a 3.2 . We can repeat the same process from the point s 3.1 that we did from the point s 1 . From the point s 3.2 , we reduce the voltage until the available resource utilization is reduced by half (ρ max -ρ 4 = ρ 4 -ρ 3 ), which is also chosen heuristically. The process is shown as arrow a 4 in Figure 2b. Again, performance is not changed in this process. From the point s 4 , we increase the resource allocation to the tasks until it reaches either s 5.1 or s 5.2 , which increases performance. From s 5.1 and s 5. 2 we can apply the same technique that was used from s 1 and s 3.2 respectively. When the start point s lies inside area D, we can apply the same technique that is used from s 2 in Figure 2a. The algorithm described above consists of two processes. One is a voltage change, and the other is an effective resource allocation change. The two processes alternate until no more improvement is possible. It is trivial to show that the algorithm converges, because effective resource allocation always increases. Since all tasks have the same voltage, the voltage change is straightforward. However, the effective resource allocation change is not trivial because each task may have a different performance function. The basic idea is that we want to improve system performance as much as possible with given energy and resource utilization. Because effective resource allocation change does not involve voltage change, this resource allocation problem is the same as was presented in [9]. The basic idea of the technique proposed in [9] is to use the first derivative of the performance functions over either resource usage ) is O(1). We adopt the same technique to increase the effective resource allocations to the tasks. It is an optimal process in the sense that the performance increase from s 2 to s 3.1 is maximal with respect to the given resource utilization. div.p: The basic idea of the search algorithm is the same as Algorithm 1 which is shown in the previous section. It starts at the same starting point where each task is given its minimum effective resource allocation and the minimum voltage. The search technique that is shown in Figure 2 is carried out except: (1) new schemes are introduced for the arrows a 2 and a 4 and ( 2) each task τ i has an independent supply voltage v i .

When a voltage is increased and decreased at arrow a 2 and arrow a 4 respectively in Figure 2, we need to choose tasks for voltage changes because each task runs at an independent voltage. Some tasks may consume less energy with the same reduction of resource utilization at a 2 , and some tasks may increase resource utilization less than others with the same energy decrease at a 4 . Since the amount of increase is limited at a 2 , the goal for a 2 is to maximize the resource utilization reduction for the given energy increase. Likewise, the goal for a 4 is to maximize the energy reduction with the given resource utilization increase. To capture these factors, we use energy density, which is the first derivative of energy consumption with respect to resource utilization. Let δ i (v i ) denote the energy density of τ i over resource see that |δ i (v i )| is monotonically increasing as v i increases where V min ≤ v i ≤ V ref , which can be drawn from the equations (Eq. 3) and (Eq. 4). The basic idea is that we increase the voltages of the tasks which increase the smallest possible energy consumption with the same resource utilization decrease. The algorithm does the following repeatedly in the case of a voltage increase such as the arrow a 2 in Figure 2: 1) choose a task or tasks with smallest |δ i (v i )|, 2) increase the voltage(s) of the task(s) until either the allowed energy budget is exhausted or |δ i (v i )| of the task(s) becomes equal to the other task(s) with the second smallest |δ i (v i )|. The detailed algorithm is presented as Algorithm 2 below. This algorithm is optimal in the sense that the reduction of resource utilization is maximized at the expense of the given energy increase. div.head: Result of the Motivational Example
div.p: The algorithm solves the motivational example. An iterative technique is used to get the value of v i from the value of |δ i (v i )|. Double precision floating point numbers are used for calculation. The search ends when both the total resource allocation and energy usage reach between 99.9% and 100% of their maximum values. The algorithm finishes the while loop in the algorithm after seven iterations. The solutions are shown in Figure 5.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we present an energy-efficient resource synthesis technique that maximizes system performance under real-time scheduling constraints and an energy budget. Two system models are considered: (1) one supply voltage for all tasks and (2) an independent supply voltages for all tasks. We proposed techniques to derive supply voltage(s) and resource allocations of the tasks in the system. Our technique considers the voltage and the effective resource share of a task as independent variables for system performance and energy consumption and derives them simultaneously. The algorithm proposed in this paper adopts an iterative method to refine the solution while energy consumption is within the limit, and real-time scheduling is possible. The iterative refining process is guaranteed to converge, and the time complexity of each iteration is as small as O(N log N). In future work, we plan to extend the resource synthesis technique to multiprocessor systems with a dynamic energy supply model.
